episodes.212323: Higher moisture along and east of the central mountain chain combined with a disturbance moving north into the state ahead of an upper low over California resulting in the development of scattered thunderstorms across the central mountain chain and nearby highlands during the afternoon and evening hours. A few storms became strong to severe resulting in nickel size hail in Santa Fe and half dollar to ping pong ball size hail in northern Union County east-northeast of Des Moines, NM.
episodes.212361: A severe thunderstorm dropped one inch diameter hail during the afternoon of May 28th.
episodes.212481: Unseasonably strong surface tracks NW to SE across Ontario, northern NY and into New England during the afternoon and evening of May 29th.
episodes.212585: An impressively moist airmass was in place with dew points well into the 60s across north-central Idaho during the afternoon, contributing to high instability. A vigorous shortwave trough pivoted northwestward through the northern Great Basin, providing strong forcing for ascent. This forcing, in conjunction with daytime heating and destabilization along the high terrain, initiated supercell thunderstorms that produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across the region.
episodes.212587: A highly unstable environment developed across western Montana, fueled by pooling moisture and steep lapse rates. Shortwave energy rotating around a broader upper-level trough provided the necessary lift for convective initiation which resulted in large hail. As storms moved into the Idaho Panhandle and interacted with the local terrain, they organized into two distinct quasi-linear convective systems, producing widespread severe wind gusts across Lincoln and Flathead Counties.
episodes.212678: Despite an upper level disturbance moving overhead on the afternoon of the 29th, only a single isolated storm developed due to mostly cloudy conditions keeping the boundary layer from becoming mixed. This one storm formed over Hall County and moved directly over Memphis producing wind gusts up to 70 mph as well as tree damage throughout town.
episodes.213026: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.
episodes.213027: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Convection was focused along the frontal boundary especially for inland locations from Waycross northward. Light northwesterly steering flow behind the boundary and abundant moisture led to slow-moving downpours.
episodes.213318: On the evening of May 27th into the morning of the 28th, plenty of atmospheric moisture and lift led to training thunderstorms across the northeastern combined Panhandles. Some flooding eventually occurred in northern Lipscomb County due to the heavy and repeated rainfall. Going into the 29th, moisture and lift continued to lead to thunderstorms, some of which became severe with hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts up to 75 to 80 mph. On the 29th, storms were mainly across the southern TX Panhandle.
episodes.213378: Weak ascent atop a very hot/unstable boundary layer fostered clusters of thunderstorms - generally disorganized/multi-cell in nature - from southwestern into north-central Oklahoma on the 29th. Damaging wind gusts and hail were observed with activity throughout the evening.
episodes.213407: A stalled upper level low pressure system resided over the western CONUS during the early morning hours of May 28, with several spokes of upper level energy moving across the Plains. This, in conjunction with a secondary upper level trough over the Great Lakes region and a slow-moving surface low pushing from the Red River into southern Nebraska led to showers and thunderstorms developing within the deep, moist airmass. As a result, multiple rounds of moderate rainfall fell over the Missouri Ozarks between May 28 and May 29, leading to widespread 3 to 4 inch rainfall accumulations. This heavy rainfall led to flooding of several low water crossings and road closures.
episodes.213471: A cluster of thunderstorms moved northeast across portions of east-central and northeast Colorado during the mid to late afternoon hours on the 29th, in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline and ahead of a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest. The highest wind gust was 66 mph in Kit Carson County, and the largest hailstone was slightly larger than quarter size in Cheyenne County.
episodes.213524: A few clusters of thunderstorms moved northeast across portions of northwest Kansas during the late afternoon and early evening hours on the 29th, in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline and ahead of a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest. A wind gust to 60 mph was reported in Sherman County, which also produced some localized blowing dust. Nickel sized hail occurred in Thomas County.
episodes.213667: A closed low in the area brought two rounds of isolated strong to severe thunderstorms to the region. The main hazard with storms was severe wind gusts.
episodes.213770: A largely cutoff shortwave low ejected through Utah late in June, resulting in isolated instances of severe wind gusts associated with convection.
episodes.214278: An approaching frontal boundary to the Natural State at the beginning of the episode would become a stationary boundary as the upper level flow pattern would begin as an approaching positively-tilted trough axis which would become an omega block and lock the mesoscale feature of the stationary boundary in position across Arkansas leading to a multiple day period of severe weather.
episodes.214392: A couple of severe thunderstorms occurred.

events.narrative: Multiple photos of oblong hail placed on top of a ruler were shared on Facebook. Another person who lives south of MT-83 reported that they lost their greenhouse and their patio furniture went flying across the patio.
Severe thunderstorm winds caused power outages for 709 customers across Idaho County. Coincident quarter-size hail was also observed.
An observer 15 miles east of Des Moines reported ping pong ball size hail from a severe thunderstorm.
The MO 95 bridge at Bryant Creek was reported to be impassable due to flooding.
The report came from mPING.
A person located one mile west of Kalispell posted a photo with multiple hailstones placed on a ruler. This thunderstorm quickly developed severe hail within 15 minutes of forming south of Kalispell.
The low water crossing by Calebs Creek was reported to be flooded due to the heavy rainfall.
A person from the public located near Woodland estimated that the winds were gusting over 60 MPH.
Over 600 customers were reported without power due to this storm.
The Santa Fe emergency manager observed nickel size hail in midtown Santa Fe from a strong thunderstorm.
An amateur radio spotter observed nickel size hail a few miles west of the Santa Fe Plaza from a strong thunderstorm.
Report relayed through social media.
Half dollar size hail was observed 9 miles east-northeast of Des Moines from a severe thunderstorm.

A quasi-linear convective system produced widespread wind damage across the county. Fallen trees blocked Highway 2 northwest of Troy, while snapped large cottonwoods caused minor damage to a carport on Missoula Avenue. Severe blowdown forced the closure of Callahan Creek Park disc golf course, and utility damage left 1,440 customers without power.

Around 2,260 customers were without power as a line of thunderstorms tracked northwards from Spotted Bear Lookout north to Glacier National Park. Also to mention, there was a storm that brought a downed tree near State Park Road in Whitefish around 1739MST on May 29, and resulted in 990 customers without power for a period of time.
Numerous roads throughout Yell County were impacted by flood waters covering roadways including the intersection of Arkansas Highway 27 and Liberty Road west of the town of Dardanelle.
Both the northbound and southbound lanes of MO 125 were closed due to flooding.
Water from heavy rainfall was over the road on State Highway T and Farm Road 75.
Several low water crossings were impassible due to the heavy rainfall.
